findings.claim: The R093 exam expects you to know every component that makes up a work plan
findings.truth: House rule: student-facing text must not carry the board's unit/spec code. The sentence reads the same without it.
findings.evidence: house rule (copyright distancing); unit brief instruction to flag any spec code in student-facing text

findings.claim: In the R093 exam, you may be given a scenario
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1.

findings.claim: Revision tip on the Gantt chart key fact: 'Recall the resolution or dimension specifications here.'
findings.truth: The box holds no resolution or dimension figures. It lists what a Gantt chart shows. The tip sends the student to recall content that is not there.

findings.claim: The R093 exam requires you to know the purpose of each document
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1.

findings.claim: In Section B of R093, you may be asked to recommend a pre-production document
findings.truth: The paper has two PARTS, not sections: Part A (10 marks) and Part B (60 marks, all questions on one scenario). 'Section B' is the wrong label, and the unit code should not appear in student text.
findings.evidence: spec 5.1 assessment overview: 'This question paper has two parts: Part A ... Part B ... All part B questions relate to a single scenario'

findings.claim: Card 4: q 'Name a key concept from 'Mind Maps and Mood Boards'.' a 'mind maps'
findings.truth: The answer repeats card 1's answer, and the question prints the answer inside it. Two flashcards in one deck must not share an answer.

findings.claim: The R093 specification covers six planning documents
findings.truth: Six is correct (asset log, flow chart, script, storyboard, visualisation diagram, wireframe layout). Only the code must go.

findings.claim: Revision tip on the asset log key fact: 'Recall the legislation and its key requirements.'
findings.truth: The box names no legislation. It says what an asset log records. The spec also states that specific Acts are not required.
findings.evidence: the box text; spec 3.4.2 'Does not include: Specific Acts of legislation'

findings.claim: Card 5: q 'Name a key concept from 'Asset Logs and Flowcharts'.' a 'asset logs'
findings.truth: Duplicate of card 1's answer, and the question prints the answer.

findings.claim: Card 5: q 'Name a key concept from 'Scripts and Storyboards'.' a 'script'
findings.truth: Duplicate of card 1's answer, and the question prints the answer.

findings.claim: shooting schedule: 'A detailed breakdown of each scene in a script ... used to organise the shooting schedule.'
findings.truth: The definition uses the term it is defining, so it explains nothing. The purpose is to organise filming.
findings.evidence: circular definition; same text repeats in the flashcard answer and the glossary

findings.claim: Both key facts carry the revision tip 'Recall the typography terms and their definitions.'
findings.truth: Neither box defines typography terms. One is about static products, the other about wireframe structure.

findings.claim: Card 4: q 'Name a key concept from 'Visualisation Diagrams and Wireframes'.' a 'visualisation diagram'
findings.truth: Duplicate of card 1's answer, and the question prints the answer.

findings.claim: Understanding camera terminology is essential for R093.
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1.

findings.claim: Both key facts carry the revision tip 'Recall the exam structure, timings, and mark allocations.'
findings.truth: Neither box gives exam structure, timing or marks. One is about shot types, the other about camera angles.

findings.claim: Card 4: q 'Name a key concept from 'Camera Shots, Angles and Movement'.' a 'camera shots'
findings.truth: Duplicate of card 1's answer, and the question prints the answer.

findings.claim: Card 2 asks for 'camera angles' but its own last sentence says 'Camera angles affect how the audience perceives power, vulnerability and status.'
findings.truth: The question hands the student the answer. Trimming the last sentence keeps the card working.

findings.claim: The R093 specification covers two areas of legal issues
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1. The two areas are correct.

findings.claim: Harassment and invasion of privacy are always illegal.
findings.truth: Harassment is against the law (Protection from Harassment Act 1997). There is no general tort or offence of invasion of privacy in English law: claims run through misuse of private information and Article 8. Filming in a public place is usually lawful, which the same box says two lines earlier. 'Always illegal' is wrong.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Privacy in English law (no general right or tort of privacy; claims brought as misuse of private information)

findings.claim: Slander - defamation in a spoken form (including interviews, podcasts and live broadcasts)
findings.truth: Words in a broadcast are libel, not slander: section 166 of the Broadcasting Act 1990 treats a programme as publication in permanent form. A recorded podcast is in permanent form too. The lesson's own libel bullet already lists broadcasts, so the two bullets contradict each other.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, English defamation law (Broadcasting Act 1990 s.166; Theatres Act 1968 s.4)

findings.claim: Revision tip on the intellectual property key fact: 'Recall the exam structure, timings, and mark allocations.'
findings.truth: The box lists copyright, trademarks and patents. It gives no exam structure or marks.

findings.claim: The R093 specification requires you to know the roles and responsibilities of four key regulatory bodies ... There are four regulatory bodies you must know: ASA, Ofcom, BBFC and PEGI.
findings.truth: The spec splits them: organisations responsible for regulation are the ASA and Ofcom; BBFC and PEGI are classification systems and certifications. Calling all four regulators is what feeds the wrong mark scheme in F25. The code must also go.
findings.evidence: spec 3.4.3 'Organisations responsible for regulation: ASA, Ofcom' / 'Classification systems and certifications: BBFC, PEGI'

findings.claim: Four regulatory bodies: ASA (adverts), Ofcom (TV/radio), BBFC (films) and PEGI (games).
findings.truth: Same split as F22.

findings.claim: Regulation and health and safety questions often appear in Section B of R093
findings.truth: The paper has Part A and Part B, not sections; Part B is the scenario part. The code must also go.

findings.claim: Q1 'Identify one regulatory body responsible for classifying media products' accepts BBFC, PEGI, ASA and Ofcom.
findings.truth: The ASA and Ofcom regulate; they do not classify products. Only the BBFC and PEGI classify. The key marks two wrong answers as correct.

findings.claim: Q3 mark scheme: 'Films cannot be shown in cinemas without a BBFC classification (1)'
findings.truth: BBFC classification is not a legal requirement for cinema. Local authorities hold the final legal authority over who may see a film in a cinema and can override the BBFC. Classification IS required by law for video and DVD supply under the Video Recordings Act 1984.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, British Board of Film Classification (local authorities have final legal authorisation; Life of Brian banned by 39 authorities; VRA 1984 supply offence)

findings.claim: Card 3 answer 'user experience'; its question opens 'The overall experience a person has ...'
findings.truth: Half the answer sits in the question. Minor, and the wording is the glossary definition, so left alone.

findings.claim: Data protection is governed by the Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR (in the glossary definition).
findings.truth: Correct for the UK, but the spec says specific Acts of legislation are not required, and the lesson body says so as well. Accurate, so no edit.
findings.evidence: spec 3.4.1 'Does not include: Specific Acts of legislation'

findings.claim: Character name - centred and in capitals ... Dialogue - centred beneath the character name
findings.truth: In standard screenplay layout both are indented blocks, not centred. 'Centred' is the usual classroom shorthand and would not be marked wrong, so no edit.

findings.claim: Card 5 answer (Creative Commons) runs to 36 words, ending 'Common types include CC BY, CC BY-NC, and CC BY-ND.'
findings.truth: A flashcard answer must be 30 words or fewer. Dropping the final sentence leaves 26 words and loses nothing: the full wording stays in the glossary and in the in-text definition.

findings.claim: BBFC ratings listed as U, PG, 12A, 12, 15, 18
findings.truth: R18 also exists (licensed cinemas and sex shops only). Incomplete, not wrong, and R18 is not needed at this level.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, British Board of Film Classification

summary: No lesson was free of findings. The real content errors are in lessons 7 and 8: 'invasion of privacy is always illegal', slander wrongly given podcasts and live broadcasts as examples (broadcasts are libel), a mark scheme that credits the ASA and Ofcom for a classification question, and a mark scheme claiming a film cannot be shown in a cinema without a BBFC certificate. The rest is hygiene: eight mentions of the board's unit code in student text, two 'Section B' labels where the paper has Part A and Part B, five placeholder flashcards that duplicate another answer in their own deck, one circular definition and seven revision tips pointing at content that is not in their box.
